Dear all,

I`m doing some modelling for social research at the moment and I came across an issue concerning the p-value of the estimator in lavaan.

In the introduction to lavaan by Mr. Y. Rosseel, a structural equation model is presented by means of the dataset "Political Democracy", including some latent variable definitions, regressions, and residual covariances (p.18ff. in this paper: http://www.jstatsoft.org/v48/i02/paper)

results for the estimator shows the following:
Estimator ML
Minimum Function Chi-square    38.125
Degrees of freedom             35
P-value                        0.329

The p-value is to my understanding not significant. How can I trust the estimated results then?
Also, further down, the residuals y4 ~~ y8 are estimated with a p of 0.431 (p.20).

I am asking this, because I am faced with a similar problem with one of my models and did not know how to interprete this, or simply ignore it.

Any help is much appreciated!

Thank you,

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: estimator - p-value (chi-square)
parts: The p-value is to my understanding not significant. How can I trust the estimated results then?

The null hypothesis for this test is that among the observed variables, the covariances/correlations implied by the model are exactly equal to the covariances/correlations among those variables in the population.  The test is conducted by comparing the observed sample covariances (and means, if those are also included in the model) to the model-implied covariances (and means, if applicable).  The alternative hypothesis is that the model-implied covariances differ from those in the population (as estimated from the sample).  In the example, we fail to reject the null, which means that the model is estimating covariances that are very similar to those in the sample, implying that our model is very similar to the true population model.  So that means we have good reason to trust the results of such a model.

As an aside, the chi-squared statistic is heavily influenced by sample size, so even trivial differences between the true population model and our hypothesized model are likely to be rejected when we have a large sample.  Because our hypothesized model does not need to be exactly correct in order to be useful, many practitioners place less emphasis on the chi-squared test than they do on some alternative indices of fit (although these indices admittedly also have their faults).  For examples of the controversy, you could peruse the articles in the 2007 special issue of the journal Personality and Individual Differences, vol. 42.
Also, further down, the residuals y4 ~~ y8 are estimated with a p of 0.431 (p.20).

The test of the correlated residuals y4 ~~ y8 is essentially independent of the test of model fit.  The null hypothesis for parameters' significance tests is the same as it is in linear regression: The slope is zero in the population.  In this case, the null hypothesis is that there is no relationship between errors of measurement for these two variables, and we fail to reject that null, so I suppose you could choose to fix that term to zero, although the fact that the parameter estimate itself is not zero simply implies that you might not have enough power to reject that null at this particular sample size (on the condition that it is not exactly zero in the population).

Terry
